text:
A new joint position statement on adult insomnia, from the Australasian Sleep Association, Sleep Health Foundation, RACGP, Australian Psychological Society, Pharmaceutical Society of Australia and Australian Primary Health Care Nurses Association, is clear: cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, known as CBTi, is the recommended first line treatment. General advice about healthy sleep habits, often called sleep hygiene, is not a sufficient stand alone treatment for chronic insomnia.

Why this matters across roles: the statement notes that CBTi is often confused with simple sleep hygiene tips, and that many people with insomnia are unaware behavioural treatments exist.

One practical takeaway: when someone says they have already had help with sleep, gently ask what that help involved. If it was a list of sleep habits, let them know CBTi exists and can be offered individually, in groups, by telehealth or through digital programs. Their GP is a good place to start, including about a Mental Health Treatment Plan.

Where the evidence stops:
• The statement covers adults, not children or adolescents.
• Not everyone responds to CBTi. Other approaches, such as mindfulness, show promise after non response.
• Access to trained clinicians is limited by waitlists and cost, and many sleep apps have little or no scientific evidence.

Key source: Sweetman et al., 2026: https://doi.org/10.1093/sleepadvances/zpag086
